title: Mary Draper Ingles escapes through Kentucky, 1755
summary: Captured by a Shawnee war party in 1755, Mary Draper Ingles was put to work making salt at Big Bone Lick in what is now Boone County before she escaped.
bodyMarkdown:
On July 30, 1755, early in the French and Indian War, a Shawnee war party struck [Draper's Meadow](https://grokipedia.com/page/Draper%27s_Meadow_massacre), a small settlement near present-day Blacksburg on the Virginia frontier. Several settlers were killed. [Mary Draper Ingles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mary_Draper_Ingles), then about twenty-three and heavily pregnant, was taken captive with her two young sons, Thomas and George, and her sister-in-law.

The captives were marched west for weeks to Shawnee towns in the Ohio country. Accounts say Mary gave birth to a daughter along the way or soon after, though the details differ between sources. Her sons were separated from her and taken into Shawnee families. George, the younger boy, died in captivity.

That autumn she was taken with a party to make salt at [Big Bone Lick](/stories/big-bone-lick-older-cycle/), in what is now Boone County. That makes her among the earliest recorded European women on Kentucky ground. At the salt camp she met an older woman, also a captive, remembered as the "old Dutch woman."

Around mid-October the two women slipped away. They had almost nothing with them. They followed the Ohio River upstream, then the Kanawha and New rivers, for roughly forty days. They ate walnuts, grapes, and roots, and they suffered from cold and hunger. Along the way the two women became separated. Mary went on alone and in early December reached a cabin near her old home on the New River. Her husband, William, had believed she was dead.

The Ingles family later ran a ferry on the New River near present-day Radford. Her son Thomas was ransomed and returned in 1768, after years among the Shawnee. Mary lived until 1815. Her escape has been retold many times since, in family accounts, books, and outdoor drama.

## Kentucky today

Big Bone Lick is now a state park in Boone County. A Kentucky Historical Society marker there notes her captivity and escape.
